I love the prophecies of Isaiah. It seems to me that he almost lived more in our day than when he was actually upon the earth. He saw so much of what would transpire in our day. He saw us settled here in these valleys of the mountains. He saw this desert, where we were once a thousand miles from transportation and supplies, made to blossom as a rose (see Isa. 35:1 [Isaiah 35:1]). He saw the rivers flow in the desert where we have built these great irrigation canals (see Isa. 43:19 [Isaiah 43:19]). He saw the water flow down from the high places where we have reservoired it in these mountain fastnesses for summer’s use (see Isa. 41:18 [Isaiah 41:18]). He saw the redeemed of the Lord come up and sing in the heights of Zion (see Isa. 51:11 [Isaiah 51:11]). And where do you find anything in the world to fulfill that like the singing of the Tabernacle Choir for over fifty years without a break?
quotes.speaker: Le Grand Richards
quotes.attr: Le Grand Richards, in Conference Report, Oct. 1980, 92; or Ensign, Nov. 1980, 64

quotes.text: In 2 Nephi 9:10, Jacob discusses the two deaths, "that monster, death and hell, which I call the death of the body, and also the death of the spirit." This commentary gives added meaning to several passages in Isaiah 51 that Jacob has just quoted in 2 Nephi 8. Isaiah writes, "Art thou not he that hath cut Rahab [i.e.,the same as Jacob's "death"], and wounded the dragon [i.e., the same as Jacob's "hell"]?" (2 Ne. 8:9). Isaiah's use of the words "ransomed" (Isa. 51:10) and "redeemed" (Isa. 51:11) takes on broader meaning as "sorrow and mourning shall flee away" (Isa. 51:11) because of the infinite Atonement that overcomes death and hell.
quotes.speaker: Garold N. Davis
quotes.attr: Garold N. Davis, "Book of Mormon Commentary on Isaiah," Ensign, Sept. 1998, 57-58
